screens.title: Storage Cost Optimization Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Storage costs grow quietly until they dominate an architecture's budget. In this lesson you will learn the practical strategies a Solutions Architect uses to keep costs under control: choosing the right S3 storage class, automating transitions with Intelligent-Tiering or Lifecycle policies, designing archives with Glacier and Deep Archive, right-sizing EBS volumes and snapshots, and using EFS Infrequent Access and the correct throughput mode. We'll ground these ideas with real examples such as moving logs through S3 tiers and pruning old EBS snapshots. You'll also learn common mistakes to avoid, like overly aggressive lifecycle rules that cause surprise retrieval charges or retaining unused snapshots forever. By the end you will be able to design a storage plan that balances access needs, retrieval times, and cost. Think of storage optimization as a set of trade-offs — lower price usually means longer retrieval or less availability — and your job is to choose the right balance for each workload. screens.title: S3 Storage Classes Overview
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing an S3 storage class is about balancing availability, retrieval time, and cost. S3 Standard is the default for frequently accessed data; it offers high availability and immediate access. Standard-Infrequent Access and One Zone-IA reduce cost for less-frequently accessed objects, with One Zone-IA storing data in a single Availability Zone for lower price but less resilience. Glacier and Glacier Deep Archive are for long-term archives where retrieval frequency is very low. Glacier makes sense when retrieval times of minutes to hours are acceptable. Deep Archive is for data accessed perhaps once a year or less, where retrieval times of hours to days are acceptable. A common misconception is that cheaper always means better; in reality, choosing a deep archive class without understanding retrieval needs can cause massive, unexpected charges if you need to restore data quickly. For example, customer transaction logs that are queried monthly should not be placed in Deep Archive. Instead, logs that must be retained only for compliance and rarely accessed are ideal candidates. Evaluate access patterns, durability needs, and regulatory requirements before selecting a class. Track expected retrieval frequency and test the retrieval process so you understand cost and latency trade-offs.

Quick comparison
S3 Standard
High availability and immediate access; use for hot data and active workloads.
Standard-IA / One Zone-IA
Lower storage cost for infrequently accessed objects; One Zone-IA lowers resilience for extra savings.
Glacier / Deep Archive
Lowest cost for long-term archives; different retrieval times and cost tiers available.
Common-mistake
Aggressive archiving without retrieval planning
Putting moderately accessed data into Deep Archive can create heavy retrieval bills and long delays when that data is needed.
Example scenarios and takeaway
Transcoding pipeline
0–60 days: S3 Standard for frequent access during processing and distribution.
Monthly audit logs
30–90 days: Standard-IA for reduced cost; 90+ days: Glacier for archival retention.
Compliance archive
Deep Archive for data rarely accessed but required long-term; test retrieval before committing.
Key Takeaway

Pick class by access frequency and retrieval tolerance. Cheaper tiers need retrieval planning.

screens.title: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
screens.narratorSegment: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between a frequent and an infrequent access tier based on observed usage. It removes the need to predict which objects will become cold and is ideal for data sets with unpredictable or changing patterns, like user-generated files or variable logs. There is a small monitoring and automation fee per object each month, so intelligent-tiering pays off when the savings from tiering exceed that fee for dynamic datasets. A concrete example: imagine an application that writes user uploads. Newly uploaded images are frequently viewed for a few days, then rarely accessed. Enabling Intelligent-Tiering avoids manual lifecycle rule management while ensuring the objects move to a lower-cost tier as their access declines. A common misconception is that Intelligent-Tiering eliminates cost considerations; you still need to check the monthly per-object automation fee and object size distribution. For very small objects or extremely high object counts, lifecycle policies or aggregation strategies may be more cost-effective. Always measure access metrics and estimate the break-even point before enabling automated tiering at scale. S3 Intelligent-Tiering means use intelligent-tiering for data with unpredictable access; weigh automation fees against expected savings.. In practical terms, automatic tiering for unknown or changing access patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Practical example

It always saves money

Key Takeaway

screens.title: S3 Lifecycle Policies
screens.narratorSegment: S3 Lifecycle policies let you define rules that transition or expire objects based on age or other criteria. They are ideal when access patterns are predictable. A typical pattern is to move objects from Standard to Standard-IA after 30 days, then to Glacier after 90 days, and finally to Deep Archive or expiration after longer retention windows. To implement this safely, create rules scoped to prefixes or tags, simulate on a test prefix, and track transitions in S3 Management metrics. An important example: log retention. Configure a lifecycle rule that targets the logs/ prefix and transitions current versions at 30, 90, and 180 days and expires at 365 days. A common mistake is setting transitions too aggressively; if data is retrieved from Glacier frequently, retrieval costs can outweigh storage savings. Another risk is applying rules to the entire bucket unintentionally. Always use narrow scope and naming conventions for rules, and document retrieval SLAs so stakeholders understand access windows. Finally, include a rule to delete incomplete multipart uploads to avoid lingering storage costs. Lifecycle policies are deterministic and transparent, making them a central cost control for planned data aging.

screens.title: Glacier and Deep Archive Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon S3 Glacier and Glacier Deep Archive provide very low-cost storage for data that is rarely accessed. The key decision is Acceptable retrieval latency versus cost. Glacier offers retrieval options with minutes-to-hours latency for flexible retrievals, and Deep Archive pushes cost down further with retrieval times measured in hours to days. Use Glacier for archives that may be retrieved a few times per year with moderate latency tolerance. Use Deep Archive when access is extremely rare, such as long-term regulatory records or scientific data that may be accessed infrequently. Always model retrieval costs: large, accidental bulk retrievals can create unexpected charges. A practical safeguard is to establish retrieval approval workflows and to test retrieval paths and timing before committing critical data. Another important point is to choose the retrieval option (expedited, standard, bulk) that fits the use case; expedited retrievals cost more but are suitable for emergency restores. Remember that storage price savings must be considered alongside eventual restore costs, retrieval time SLAs, and any business processes that require timely access. Glacier and Deep Archive Considerations means glacier and deep archive are cheapest for very low access frequency but require retrieval planning and approval to avoid surprise costs.. In practical terms, low-cost long-term storage and retrieval trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Glacier & Deep Archive
When to choose each
If data is accessed once a quarter or less, Glacier can be appropriate; if access is once a year or less, Deep Archive yields further savings. Always align retrieval time expectations with business needs.
Glacier retrievals
Multiple retrieval options: expedited for urgent needs, standard and bulk for cost savings. Test each and understand cost differences.
Deep Archive use cases
Long-term compliance, raw research data, or media that will not be accessed frequently. Ensure retrieval time is acceptable before committing.
Examples and safeguards
Archive of completed projects that rarely need restores; assign retrieval approval and monitor request volumes.
Avoid placing active datasets into Deep Archive; retrieval can be slow and expensive if mistaken.
Use retrieval testing and small restore trials to estimate both time and cost before large-scale retention decisions.
Key Takeaway

Archive aggressively only when retrievals are rare and well understood. Test retrieval types and estimate restore cost and latency.

screens.title: EBS Right-Sizing and Volume Types
screens.narratorSegment: EBS costs are directly tied to provisioned volume size and type. Right-sizing means provisioning the smallest volume that meets capacity needs, and choosing a volume type that provides required IOPS and throughput without overpaying. For many workloads, gp3 is cost-effective because it separates baseline storage from IOPS and throughput, allowing independent scaling. For high-performance databases, io2 or io2 Block Express may be required for durable high IOPS. Throughput-intensive workloads such as big data streaming may benefit from st1. To right-size, monitor disk utilization and IOPS with CloudWatch, identify persistent underutilization, and shrink or migrate volumes where safe. A typical workflow is to snapshot the volume, create a smaller volume from a snapshot if possible, or migrate to a new instance with an appropriately sized volume. Avoid creating a 1TB volume when 100GB suffices. A common pitfall is resizing without testing: always snapshot before changing sizes, and validate performance after the change. Regularly review volume types and usage patterns to adjust choices as workloads evolve. EBS Right-Sizing and Volume Types means measure utilization, choose a balanced volume type like gp3 when suitable, and test changes with snapshots to avoid downtime.. In practical terms, select the right ebs volume and scale only what you need. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › EBS Right-Sizing
Volume types and when to use them
  • gp3: general purpose, independent IOPS/throughput scaling — often most cost-effective.
  • io2 / io2 Block Express: high performance and durability for databases.
  • st1: throughput-optimized for large sequential workloads.
Right-sizing checklist
Monitor usage, snapshot before change, perform a test resize or migration, and confirm application behavior and costs post-change.
Example
A database was provisioned with a 1TB gp3 but shows steady 200GB usage. After validating IOPS and throughput needs, the architect snapshots the volume, provisions a 250GB gp3 with matching IOPS, switches the instance to the new volume, and observes no performance loss while saving monthly storage costs.
Key Takeaway

Measure before you change. Choose gp3 for many use cases and reserve io2 or st1 for specialized performance needs.

screens.title: EBS Snapshot Lifecycle Management
screens.narratorSegment: EBS snapshots are incremental backups that live in S3 and can accumulate into substantial costs if not managed. A practical snapshot lifecycle strategy includes automated creation, retention policies, and scheduled deletion. Start by automating snapshot creation using AWS Backup or Data Lifecycle Manager so backups exist regularly and consistently. Next, implement deletion rules: keep daily snapshots for a short window, weekly for a medium window, and monthly for long-term retention as required by policy. Regularly review snapshot lists to delete orphaned snapshots and consider snapshot archive features where available to move older snapshots to lower-cost archive tiers. A common mistake is retaining every snapshot forever “just in case.” This quickly balloons costs and creates noise during restores. Another important practice is to tag snapshots with owner, purpose, and retention expiry so automation can safely remove expired snapshots. Always test the restore process from a snapshot or archive to ensure your backups are useful, and track backup storage in Cost Explorer to measure benefit versus expense. EBS Snapshot Lifecycle Management means automate creation and deletion, tag assets, and test restores to avoid accumulating costly, stale backups.. In practical terms, automate backups, purge old snapshots, and consider snapshot archive. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Automate and tag
Use DLM or AWS Backup to schedule snapshots. Tag snapshots with owner, retention policy, and purpose so automated deletions are safe and auditable.
Retention tiers
  • Daily snapshots: keep 7–14 days.
  • Weekly snapshots: keep several weeks to months.
  • Monthly snapshots: keep according to compliance.

Snapshots are incremental but still cost money. Automate lifecycle and tag everything so you can remove expired backups confidently.

screens.title: Amazon EFS: Infrequent Access & Throughput Modes
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon EFS supports lifecycle management that moves files to an Infrequent Access tier when they haven't been used for a set period. This is highly effective for mixed-access shared file systems—developer home directories and content repositories often contain cold files alongside active files. Enabling EFS IA moves dormant files to a lower-cost tier without changing how applications access files. On throughput, EFS offers bursting mode and provisioned mode. Bursting is cost-effective for workloads that are usually idle but occasionally require high throughput. Provisioned mode is appropriate when you have consistent, predictable throughput needs and want guaranteed performance. A common mistake is leaving EFS in a single configuration when workloads change; you should review access patterns and switch modes if behavior becomes steady. For example, a build artifact store that only spikes during nightly builds can stay in bursting mode, but a CI system with constant heavy traffic may need provisioned throughput. Combine EFS IA with appropriate throughput settings to minimize storage and performance costs simultaneously. screens.title: Continuous Storage Audit

Regularly scan for unattached EBS volumes and delete them when they are not needed; these volumes incur charges even when not attached. Look for old or empty S3 buckets and large objects that have outlived their purpose, and apply lifecycle rules or delete them. For snapshots, list snapshots older than a threshold and validate whether they are required; then delete or archive them. Tagging resources with owner and purpose helps automation and human reviewers decide what to keep. Schedule monthly or quarterly audits, create a peer-review step for deletions in case of mistakes, and maintain documentation for retention policies tied to compliance needs. A common oversight is ignoring incremental storage like failed multipart uploads; create a lifecycle rule to delete incomplete multipart uploads after a week. screens.title: Implementing S3 Lifecycle Policies — Step-by-Step

fullNarratorScript:
Storage costs grow quietly until they dominate an architecture's budget. In this lesson you will learn the practical strategies a Solutions Architect uses to keep costs under control: choosing the right S3 storage class, automating transitions with Intelligent-Tiering or Lifecycle policies, designing archives with Glacier and Deep Archive, right-sizing EBS volumes and snapshots, and using EFS Infrequent Access and the correct throughput mode. We'll ground these ideas with real examples such as moving logs through S3 tiers and pruning old EBS snapshots. You'll also learn common mistakes to avoid, like overly aggressive lifecycle rules that cause surprise retrieval charges or retaining unused snapshots forever. By the end you will be able to design a storage plan that balances access needs, retrieval times, and cost. Think of storage optimization as a set of trade-offs — lower price usually means longer retrieval or less availability — and your job is to choose the right balance for each workload. Ready to explore the key topics and practical steps that make those trade-offs safe and auditable?

In this segment we make the objectives concrete. You will learn to implement S3 Intelligent-Tiering and lifecycle policies so objects automatically move to lower-cost storage when access patterns change. We'll practice designing S3 Glacier and Deep Archive strategies for long-term compliance archives and understand retrieval trade-offs. You will master EBS cost controls by right-sizing volumes, selecting the appropriate volume type for IOPS and throughput needs, and creating a snapshot lifecycle that avoids indefinite retention. Finally, you'll apply EFS optimization techniques: enable Infrequent Access to lower storage cost for dormant files and choose bursting or provisioned throughput based on workload patterns. Each objective ties to a competency milestone: configuring policies, proving cost savings in Cost Explorer, and cleaning unused resources. You will also learn to spot and remove common sources of waste like unattached volumes or forgotten buckets. These skills are practical: they'll reduce recurring bills and make designs predictable for finance and compliance. By the end you will be able to demonstrate each competency with a small example or audit.

These milestone cards turn objectives into repeatable actions. First, you will deploy S3 Intelligent-Tiering for datasets with unknown or changing access patterns so objects move between frequent and infrequent tiers automatically. This is valuable when you cannot predict access windows, like logs or user uploads. Second, you will author lifecycle policies for known patterns; an example is transitioning objects to Standard-IA after 30 days, Glacier after 90 days, and expiring after 365 days. Third, you will audit and right-size EBS volumes: measure actual usage with monitoring, change sizes where appropriate, and select cost-effective volume types like gp3 for many general workloads. Fourth, you will enable EFS lifecycle management to move files to Infrequent Access after a retention period and choose throughput mode to match bursty or steady workloads. Each milestone includes a verification step such as confirming transitions in S3 metrics or showing snapshot deletion in AWS Backup logs. These are repeatable checks that prove you reduced risk and monthly cost without impeding required access.

Choosing an S3 storage class is about balancing availability, retrieval time, and cost. S3 Standard is the default for frequently accessed data; it offers high availability and immediate access. Standard-Infrequent Access and One Zone-IA reduce cost for less-frequently accessed objects, with One Zone-IA storing data in a single Availability Zone for lower price but less resilience. Glacier and Glacier Deep Archive are for long-term archives where retrieval frequency is very low. Glacier makes sense when retrieval times of minutes to hours are acceptable. Deep Archive is for data accessed perhaps once a year or less, where retrieval times of hours to days are acceptable. A common misconception is that cheaper always means better; in reality, choosing a deep archive class without understanding retrieval needs can cause massive, unexpected charges if you need to restore data quickly. For example, customer transaction logs that are queried monthly should not be placed in Deep Archive. Instead, logs that must be retained only for compliance and rarely accessed are ideal candidates. Evaluate access patterns, durability needs, and regulatory requirements before selecting a class. Track expected retrieval frequency and test the retrieval process so you understand cost and latency trade-offs.

S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between a frequent and an infrequent access tier based on observed usage. It removes the need to predict which objects will become cold and is ideal for data sets with unpredictable or changing patterns, like user-generated files or variable logs. There is a small monitoring and automation fee per object each month, so intelligent-tiering pays off when the savings from tiering exceed that fee for dynamic datasets. A concrete example: imagine an application that writes user uploads. Newly uploaded images are frequently viewed for a few days, then rarely accessed. Enabling Intelligent-Tiering avoids manual lifecycle rule management while ensuring the objects move to a lower-cost tier as their access declines. A common misconception is that Intelligent-Tiering eliminates cost considerations; you still need to check the monthly per-object automation fee and object size distribution. For very small objects or extremely high object counts, lifecycle policies or aggregation strategies may be more cost-effective. Always measure access metrics and estimate the break-even point before enabling automated tiering at scale. S3 Intelligent-Tiering means use intelligent-tiering for data with unpredictable access; weigh automation fees against expected savings.. In practical terms, automatic tiering for unknown or changing access patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

S3 Lifecycle policies let you define rules that transition or expire objects based on age or other criteria. They are ideal when access patterns are predictable. A typical pattern is to move objects from Standard to Standard-IA after 30 days, then to Glacier after 90 days, and finally to Deep Archive or expiration after longer retention windows. To implement this safely, create rules scoped to prefixes or tags, simulate on a test prefix, and track transitions in S3 Management metrics. An important example: log retention. Configure a lifecycle rule that targets the logs/ prefix and transitions current versions at 30, 90, and 180 days and expires at 365 days. A common mistake is setting transitions too aggressively; if data is retrieved from Glacier frequently, retrieval costs can outweigh storage savings. Another risk is applying rules to the entire bucket unintentionally. Always use narrow scope and naming conventions for rules, and document retrieval SLAs so stakeholders understand access windows. Finally, include a rule to delete incomplete multipart uploads to avoid lingering storage costs. Lifecycle policies are deterministic and transparent, making them a central cost control for planned data aging.

Amazon S3 Glacier and Glacier Deep Archive provide very low-cost storage for data that is rarely accessed. The key decision is Acceptable retrieval latency versus cost. Glacier offers retrieval options with minutes-to-hours latency for flexible retrievals, and Deep Archive pushes cost down further with retrieval times measured in hours to days. Use Glacier for archives that may be retrieved a few times per year with moderate latency tolerance. Use Deep Archive when access is extremely rare, such as long-term regulatory records or scientific data that may be accessed infrequently. Always model retrieval costs: large, accidental bulk retrievals can create unexpected charges. A practical safeguard is to establish retrieval approval workflows and to test retrieval paths and timing before committing critical data. Another important point is to choose the retrieval option (expedited, standard, bulk) that fits the use case; expedited retrievals cost more but are suitable for emergency restores. Remember that storage price savings must be considered alongside eventual restore costs, retrieval time SLAs, and any business processes that require timely access. Glacier and Deep Archive Considerations means glacier and deep archive are cheapest for very low access frequency but require retrieval planning and approval to avoid surprise costs.. In practical terms, low-cost long-term storage and retrieval trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

EBS costs are directly tied to provisioned volume size and type. Right-sizing means provisioning the smallest volume that meets capacity needs, and choosing a volume type that provides required IOPS and throughput without overpaying. For many workloads, gp3 is cost-effective because it separates baseline storage from IOPS and throughput, allowing independent scaling. For high-performance databases, io2 or io2 Block Express may be required for durable high IOPS. Throughput-intensive workloads such as big data streaming may benefit from st1. To right-size, monitor disk utilization and IOPS with CloudWatch, identify persistent underutilization, and shrink or migrate volumes where safe. A typical workflow is to snapshot the volume, create a smaller volume from a snapshot if possible, or migrate to a new instance with an appropriately sized volume. Avoid creating a 1TB volume when 100GB suffices. A common pitfall is resizing without testing: always snapshot before changing sizes, and validate performance after the change. Regularly review volume types and usage patterns to adjust choices as workloads evolve. EBS Right-Sizing and Volume Types means measure utilization, choose a balanced volume type like gp3 when suitable, and test changes with snapshots to avoid downtime.. In practical terms, select the right ebs volume and scale only what you need. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

EBS snapshots are incremental backups that live in S3 and can accumulate into substantial costs if not managed. A practical snapshot lifecycle strategy includes automated creation, retention policies, and scheduled deletion. Start by automating snapshot creation using AWS Backup or Data Lifecycle Manager so backups exist regularly and consistently. Next, implement deletion rules: keep daily snapshots for a short window, weekly for a medium window, and monthly for long-term retention as required by policy. Regularly review snapshot lists to delete orphaned snapshots and consider snapshot archive features where available to move older snapshots to lower-cost archive tiers. A common mistake is retaining every snapshot forever “just in case.” This quickly balloons costs and creates noise during restores. Another important practice is to tag snapshots with owner, purpose, and retention expiry so automation can safely remove expired snapshots. Always test the restore process from a snapshot or archive to ensure your backups are useful, and track backup storage in Cost Explorer to measure benefit versus expense. EBS Snapshot Lifecycle Management means automate creation and deletion, tag assets, and test restores to avoid accumulating costly, stale backups.. In practical terms, automate backups, purge old snapshots, and consider snapshot archive. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Amazon EFS supports lifecycle management that moves files to an Infrequent Access tier when they haven't been used for a set period. This is highly effective for mixed-access shared file systems—developer home directories and content repositories often contain cold files alongside active files. Enabling EFS IA moves dormant files to a lower-cost tier without changing how applications access files. On throughput, EFS offers bursting mode and provisioned mode. Bursting is cost-effective for workloads that are usually idle but occasionally require high throughput. Provisioned mode is appropriate when you have consistent, predictable throughput needs and want guaranteed performance. A common mistake is leaving EFS in a single configuration when workloads change; you should review access patterns and switch modes if behavior becomes steady. Let's recap the most important concepts. First, S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers based on usage and is best when access patterns are unpredictable, but remember the per-object automation fee. Second, S3 Lifecycle policies provide deterministic transitions and expirations for known patterns and are excellent for log aging and compliance retention. Third, Amazon S3 Glacier and Glacier Deep Archive are the most cost-effective for long-term archives, but retrieval times and costs differ significantly, so always test restores and plan approval workflows. These three points are the heart of storage cost optimization in S3: match access frequency to the right storage class, automate transitions safely, and plan retrieval governance for archives. Keep these concepts in mind as you implement policies and audits because they balance recurring cost savings against operational requirements.

Now the storage components beyond S3. First, EBS volumes should be right-sized and matched to workload IOPS and throughput; gp3 often provides the best balance for general workloads while io2 suits high-performance databases. Second, snapshots are incremental backups stored in S3; automate snapshot creation and deletion with DLM or AWS Backup and tag snapshots so expired backups can be removed safely. Third, Amazon EFS supports Infrequent Access to reduce costs for dormant files and has throughput modes to match bursty or constant demand. Finally, continuous auditing for unattached EBS volumes, stale buckets, incomplete multipart uploads, and old snapshots prevents silent cost accumulation. Tagging, automation, testing restores, and governance tie all of these together. Treat storage optimization as an ongoing operational practice, not a one-time activity.
